name: Profhilo / skin booster injectables

lead: Profhilo is an injectable hyaluronic acid made by IBSA and sold in Europe since 2015. It is meant to improve skin quality, hydration and elasticity rather than add volume, and belongs to the wider 'skin booster' category.
Evidence is mostly small open-label studies and post-marketing safety data.

paras: It combines high and low molecular weight HA, proposed to stimulate fibroblasts to produce collagen and elastin and to hydrate the dermis.
Reported effects are mostly minor: swelling, redness, bruising. HA injectables can rarely cause vascular occlusion. A source states it was not FDA-approved as of January 2026.

lead: Profhilo is an injectable hyaluronic acid (HA) product made by IBSA Derma, launched in Europe in 2015, that is marketed as a skin 'bio-remodelling' treatment rather than a volume filler.[1][2] Each syringe combines high and low molecular weight HA stabilised by a heat process, with no chemical cross-linker.[1]

It belongs to a broader category called skin boosters: injectables placed in the dermis to improve hydration, elasticity and texture instead of adding volume. A 2024 review traces how the term evolved from HA fillers and notes that definitions of the category vary.[3]
Evidence consists mainly of small open-label studies and post-marketing data. As of January 2026, one source states that Profhilo was not FDA-approved in the US.[1]
infobox: High and low molecular weight hyaluronic acid, non-cross-linked[1]
CE-marked device in EU; not FDA-approved as of January 2026 per source[1]

paras: Each 2 ml syringe is reported to hold 64 mg of HA, half high molecular weight and half low, combined by IBSA's patented NAHYCO process.[1] Proponents describe 'hybrid cooperative complexes' that they say activate cellular processes in skin, a concept examined in a 2016 laboratory paper.[4] The product is used on the face, neck and body, and a typical course is described as two sessions about 30 days apart followed by maintenance.[1]
Skin boosters as a class include HA, polynucleotides and other materials, and reviews discuss their types and mechanisms.[3][5]

Small open-label studies of roughly 11 to 64 participants report gains in hydration, elasticity and wrinkle scores lasting up to about six months, according to one source.[1] An expert panel consensus on stabilised HA skin boosters has also been published, and reviews evaluate the evidence for the category as mixed in quality.[5][6]

A worldwide post-marketing safety assessment of Profhilo, on the market since 2015, covers tens of thousands of patients.[2] One source reports that most events were minor and transient, such as swelling, redness and bruising.[1] HA injectables generally carry risks of bruising, nodules and, rarely, vascular occlusion.[7]

Registered Profhilo studies include a trial in malar and sub-malar volume deficiency (n=64), neck (n=25), inner arm and abdomen (n=24), back of the hands (n=51), and Profhilo Structura (n=164).[8][9][10][11][12] A 2024 single-arm pilot study evaluated intradermal HA as a skin quality booster.[13]
